title: Đề luyện Đọc VSTEP — Recall SGU0822 (3 passage)

passages.p1:
Rebecca Vaughan was, until recently, a name known only to a small circle of literary editors. That changed with the publication of her second novel, "The Quiet Harbour," a book that has been described as one of the most assured works of fiction to appear in years. The story follows Marianne Elde, a retired lighthouse keeper who returns to the remote coastal village where she grew up, only to discover that the community she remembers has been quietly dismantled by the closing of its fishing industry. Rather than a plot driven by dramatic events, the novel is a study of absence — of how people carry the shape of vanished places inside them. Its central concerns are memory, belonging, and the stubborn human habit of romanticising the past.

Vaughan has been candid about where the story began. She grew up in a fishing town on the north-east coast, and as a teenager she watched the harbour empty year by year as boats were sold and families moved inland in search of work. "I wasn't trying to write a documentary," she has said, "but I couldn't shake the image of a place slowly forgetting itself." The decisive moment, however, came not during her childhood but much later, when she returned to the town for her grandmother's funeral and found the old quayside converted into a car park. That single afternoon, she has explained, handed her the emotional centre of the book. She began drafting the opening chapter on the train home.

What distinguishes the novel, many have argued, is its restraint. Vaughan resists tidy resolutions: Marianne never fully reconciles with her estranged brother, and the village is not rescued by any late intervention. Instead the book lingers on small, precise observations — the smell of tar, the particular grey of a winter sea — that accumulate into something quietly devastating. Some early readers found this deliberate slowness frustrating, and Vaughan herself concedes that the novel "asks for patience." Yet most reviewers have treated that patience as the whole point rather than a weakness.

Critical reaction has been strikingly warm. The Herald called it "a masterclass in what a writer chooses to leave unsaid," while a reviewer for the weekend edition of The Chronicle praised Vaughan's "unfashionable faith in ordinary lives." Not every notice was unqualified — one critic complained that the secondary characters were too lightly sketched — but even that reviewer conceded the writing itself was accomplished. Journalist Tom Hedley, profiling the author for a national newspaper, remarked that Vaughan "writes about loss without ever tipping into sentimentality," a balance he judged genuinely rare among her contemporaries.

Readers, too, have embraced the book, though in a slow, word-of-mouth way rather than through any immediate surge in sales. On one popular reading forum, a retired teacher wrote that the novel "made me phone my sister for the first time in three years" — a reaction Vaughan says moved her more than any professional review. Booksellers in coastal towns report that the novel sells especially well to older customers who recognise their own communities in its pages. Vaughan is now at work on a third book and, although she refuses to discuss its subject, she admits it will once again be set beside the sea. For a writer who spent a decade being politely overlooked, the transformation has been sudden — but, she insists, she is in no hurry to repeat it.
passages.p2:
The overwhelming majority of deaf children — by some estimates more than nine in ten — are born to hearing parents, and most of those parents have never had reason to learn a sign language. This demographic fact, easily overlooked, sits at the root of a problem that linguists regard as one of the most instructive natural experiments in the study of the human mind. A hearing child absorbs the language spoken around them almost effortlessly in the first years of life; a deaf child in a hearing household, by contrast, may be surrounded by speech they cannot access and by no visual language at all. Unless someone intervenes, such a child can reach school age without ever having acquired a complete first language of any kind.

What these children typically do develop is something researchers call homesign: a private repertoire of invented gestures worked out between the child and immediate family. Homesign is a genuine achievement and should not be dismissed. It allows a child to request food, refer to absent objects, and comment on events, and its gestures are not merely random pantomime but show consistent, rule-like patterns. Yet it falls short of a full language in ways that matter. Its vocabulary is small, its grammar rudimentary, and — crucially — it is shared with no one beyond the household that improvised it. A homesigner cannot walk into another family's home and be understood, because the system was never a communal possession to begin with.

The distinction the passage insists upon is therefore not between gesture and speech but between an idiosyncratic code and a true language. Established sign languages such as American Sign Language are languages in the full technical sense: they possess their own grammar, their own regional variation, and a community of users who transmit them across generations. They are not, as a stubborn misconception holds, manual versions of the surrounding spoken language, nor are they universal; a signer of one may be as lost with another as any two speakers of unrelated tongues. Where a stable community of signers exists, a child born into it acquires that language on the ordinary timetable, with none of the deprivation described above.

The stakes of missing that early window are considerable. Language acquisition appears to be governed by a sensitive period, a stretch of early childhood during which the brain takes to a first language with a readiness it never quite recovers later. Children who receive their first full language late — whether a late-signed one or, after cochlear implantation, a late-heard one — tend on average to attain it less completely than those exposed from infancy, and the gap can persist into adulthood. Because so much later learning, including reading, is scaffolded on an existing first language, the consequences ripple outward into literacy and, some argue, into domains of thought that depend on language as a tool. Researchers are careful here: the claim is not that a late learner is doomed, still less that the deaf are cognitively deficient, but that early, full access to some language — signed or spoken — matters, and that its absence exacts a measurable cost.

That qualification is easy to miss and worth dwelling on, because the history of deaf education is littered with the opposite assumption. For over a century many schools actively suppressed signing in the belief that it impeded speech, a policy that in hindsight often withheld from children the very thing — an accessible first language — they most needed. The modern lesson drawn from homesign and from the sensitive period is almost the reverse: what a deaf child requires is not a particular modality but timely immersion in a complete language, by whatever channel the child can receive it. On that single point the evidence has become difficult to dispute.
passages.p3:
For the better part of two decades, Facebook was almost a synonym for social media itself. To take part in the internet's conversation, a newcomer first built a profile there. Yet a quiet reversal is now under way, and it is not the dramatic collapse that commentators periodically forecast. The change is easy to miss precisely because it involves no scandal and no sudden exodus, only a gradual tilting of the balance. The platform's difficulty is subtler and, for its owners, far more awkward to solve: Facebook is growing old. Its total membership keeps climbing year after year, but the average age of the people behind those accounts is drifting steadily upward, and the youngest generation of internet users is drifting away.

The figures tell an unglamorous story. Where the site once teemed with students, it is now sustained increasingly by their parents and grandparents. Members of Generation X and the baby-boom generation not only make up a swelling share of the audience but also sign in more often and linger longer than almost anyone born after the mid-1990s. For these older users the network supplies precisely what they came for: photographs of relatives, neighbourhood groups, items for sale, and a dependable stream of news. The very features that reassure them, however, are exactly what younger visitors find off-putting.

Ask a teenager why the app stays closed on their phone and the answers come fast. The interface feels crowded and dated, an attic stuffed with notifications nobody requested. Advertisements and recycled articles crowd out the friends the service was supposedly built around. Most decisive of all is the social awkwardness of sharing a space with aunts, uncles and former teachers, whose watchful presence makes any post feel monitored. What once promised effortless connection now feels like performing under supervision. Privacy, or at least the comfortable illusion of it, has evaporated, and with it the sense that anything posted is genuine rather than polished for an audience of distant acquaintances.

Their attention has migrated elsewhere, chiefly toward Snapchat and Instagram. Snapchat's pull is especially instructive. Messages and pictures there are designed to vanish, and that impermanence is the whole point: an image that erases itself after a single glance carries no demand for polish and leaves behind no permanent record to be judged against later. For a generation raised on the anxiety of the permanent post, that promise of forgetting is a quiet relief. Communication becomes playful and visual — a silly face, a fleeting mood — rather than a broadcast aimed at hundreds. Above all, the app is built for a handful of close friends instead of a crowd, restoring the intimacy that Facebook, in its sprawling maturity, mislaid long ago. Where the older network invites you to announce, Snapchat invites you simply to share a moment and let it disappear.

None of this means the giant is finished. Measured by revenue and by the sheer scale of its user base, Facebook remains, for now, comfortably the king; billions of people still pass through it every month, and advertisers dutifully follow the crowd. What is slipping is harder to count than money — cultural relevance among the young, the intangible sense that a place is where things actually happen. A company can be enormously profitable and quietly unfashionable at the same time, and history suggests that the second condition tends, sooner or later, to threaten the first. Rivals that once looked invincible have faded before, and faster than anyone expected. Whether Facebook can grow old gracefully, or whether age is merely the opening chapter of a longer decline, remains genuinely uncertain.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What does the passage suggest about Rebecca Vaughan's reputation before her second novel appeared?
options: A. She had already collected several major literary awards.
B. She was recognised by only a handful of people in publishing.
C. She was utterly unknown to everyone in the book world.
D. She was popular chiefly among readers in coastal towns.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 1 nói tên bà "chỉ được biết đến trong một nhóm nhỏ các biên tập viên văn học," tức chỉ một số ít người trong ngành. Đáp án C sai vì quá tuyệt đối, còn D là chi tiết ở đoạn cuối chứ không phải giai đoạn trước đó.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What is the novel "The Quiet Harbour" mainly about?
options: A. A lighthouse keeper who uncovers a crime in a busy port.
B. A fishing community that is saved by a brand-new industry.
C. A young woman who leaves her village to work in the city.
D. An older woman facing how her childhood village has faded away.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 1 cho biết Marianne, người gác hải đăng về hưu, trở về làng cũ và thấy cộng đồng đã tan rã do ngành cá đóng cửa — tức đối diện với sự mai một của nơi chốn tuổi thơ. Các phương án khác đảo ngược hoặc gán sai chi tiết.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

In paragraph 1, the word "dismantled" is closest in meaning to
options: A. broken apart
B. put back together
C. openly celebrated
D. made much larger
questions.explanation: "Dismantled" ở đây chỉ việc cộng đồng bị rã ra, tan vỡ vì ngành đánh cá đóng cửa; nghĩa gần nhất là "bị phá vỡ." Các lựa chọn còn lại mang nghĩa ngược lại hoặc không liên quan.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

According to Vaughan, what finally gave the novel its emotional core?
options: A. The years she spent as a teenager watching boats being sold.
B. A long talk with her grandmother about the town's history.
C. A visit for a funeral, when she saw the old quay turned into parking.
D. A television documentary about declining fishing towns.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 2 nói "khoảnh khắc quyết định" đến khi bà về dự đám tang bà ngoại và thấy bến tàu thành bãi đỗ xe, chính buổi chiều đó trao cho bà trung tâm cảm xúc. Phương án A đúng một nửa nhưng đó là thời thơ ấu, không phải khoảnh khắc quyết định.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

In paragraph 3, the phrase "that patience" refers to
options: A. the reviewers' willingness to forgive weak characters
B. the slow, unhurried reading the novel demands of its audience
C. Vaughan's long wait to be noticed as a writer
D. Marianne's tolerance towards her estranged brother
questions.explanation: Ngay trước đó, đoạn 3 mô tả "sự chậm rãi có chủ ý" và việc cuốn sách "đòi hỏi sự kiên nhẫn"; "that patience" chính là trải nghiệm đọc chậm mà tác phẩm yêu cầu. Các phương án khác lấy từ khóa ở chỗ khác của bài.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

Which statement about the novel's ending is supported by the passage?
options: A. The village's decline is not reversed by any last event.
B. Marianne at last mends her bond with her brother.
C. The fishing trade is revived by the community's efforts.
D. Marianne decides to leave the village permanently.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 3 khẳng định Vaughan tránh những cái kết gọn gàng: làng "không được cứu vãn bởi bất kỳ sự can thiệp muộn màng nào." Các phương án B và C nói ngược lại tinh thần tiết chế của tác phẩm.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

The passage mentions all of the following reactions to the novel EXCEPT:
options: A. praise for how much the author leaves unspoken
B. admiration for her interest in unremarkable lives
C. a complaint that the minor characters felt underdeveloped
D. criticism that the prose itself was clumsy and weak
questions.explanation: Đoạn 4 nêu lời khen về điều "không nói ra," về "những cuộc đời bình dị," và lời phàn nàn về nhân vật phụ; nhưng ngay nhà phê bình đó cũng thừa nhận "lối viết là điêu luyện," nên chê văn vụng về là điều KHÔNG được nhắc đến.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What did journalist Tom Hedley particularly admire about Vaughan's writing?
options: A. her taste for emotional, tear-jerking scenes
B. her preference for dramatic, event-packed plots
C. her way of handling sorrow without slipping into mawkishness
D. how closely her style resembled other writers of her time
questions.explanation: Hedley khen Vaughan "viết về mất mát mà không bao giờ sa vào ủy mị" — tức xử lý nỗi buồn có kiềm chế. Phương án D trái ngược, vì ông cho rằng sự cân bằng đó "hiếm có trong số những người cùng thời."

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What can be inferred about how the book reached its readers?
options: A. Its readership grew gradually through personal recommendation.
B. It became a bestseller right after it was released.
C. It sold best to young professionals living in cities.
D. It was pushed hard through newspaper advertising.
questions.explanation: Đoạn cuối nói độc giả đón nhận sách "theo kiểu chậm rãi, truyền miệng chứ không phải qua cú tăng doanh số tức thời" — tức lan dần nhờ giới thiệu. Phương án B, C đảo ngược chi tiết (không tăng vọt; khách lớn tuổi ven biển, không phải giới trẻ thành phố).

questions.content:
reading — Passage 1

What does the final paragraph suggest about Vaughan's attitude towards her sudden success?
options: A. She is eager to grow famous again as fast as she can.
B. She deeply regrets the years she spent being overlooked.
C. She intends to give up coastal settings in future books.
D. She feels settled and in no rush to recreate the surge.
questions.explanation: Đoạn cuối kết bằng lời bà "không hề vội vàng muốn lặp lại nó," cho thấy thái độ điềm tĩnh. Phương án C trái ngược vì bà thừa nhận cuốn tiếp theo "sẽ lại lấy bối cảnh bên bờ biển."

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: A. To argue that homesign deserves to be recognised as a language fully equal to ASL.
B. To show why receiving a complete language early is so important, using deaf children as the case.
C. To trace how American Sign Language developed and spread across successive generations.
D. To compare the grammatical structure of signed languages with that of spoken languages.
questions.explanation: Bài xoay quanh việc trẻ điếc minh họa cho một luận điểm rộng hơn: cần tiếp cận sớm với một ngôn ngữ đầy đủ. Các phương án còn lại chỉ chạm tới một chi tiết phụ (ASL, so sánh ngữ pháp) hoặc nói ngược ý tác giả về ký hiệu nhà.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

According to the passage, most deaf children are born into families that
options: A. already use a regional sign language at home.
B. have opted for cochlear implantation very early on.
C. include at least one parent who is also deaf.
D. have never previously become familiar with any signing system.
questions.explanation: Bài nêu cha mẹ nghe được và 'chưa bao giờ có lý do để học một ngôn ngữ ký hiệu'. Các phương án A và C nói ngược thực tế đó; B là chi tiết được nhắc ở chỗ khác nhưng không phải đặc điểm chung của các gia đình này.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

In the second paragraph, the word "rudimentary" (describing homesign's grammar) is closest in meaning to
options: A. basic and only partly developed.
B. strict and tightly bound by rules.
C. borrowed directly from spoken speech.
D. constantly shifting and unstable.
questions.explanation: Bài đặt 'rudimentary' cạnh 'vốn từ nhỏ' để nói ngữ pháp còn sơ khai, chưa đầy đủ. B và C bám vào các từ khóa khác trong đoạn (có tính quy tắc; phiên bản của tiếng nói) nhưng lệch nghĩa của chính từ này.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

In the final paragraph, the phrase "the very thing … they most needed" refers to
options: A. the capacity to produce clear spoken words.
B. formal instruction in reading and writing.
C. a full first language they could genuinely absorb while still young.
D. a place at a specialised school for deaf pupils.
questions.explanation: Cụm gạch nối ngay sau đó chú thích chính nó là 'một ngôn ngữ mẹ đẻ có thể tiếp cận được'. A bám từ khóa 'tiếng nói'; D bám 'trường học'; B suy diễn xa hơn điều bài nói.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

The passage suggests that homesign differs from a full language mainly because it
options: A. consists of random gestures showing no consistent patterns.
B. can be understood only inside the household that devised it.
C. cannot be used to talk about objects that are not present.
D. depends on the grammar of the surrounding spoken language.
questions.explanation: Điểm 'then chốt' bài nêu là ký hiệu nhà không được chia sẻ với ai ngoài gia đình đã ứng biến ra nó. A và C nói ngược bài (cử chỉ có tính quy tắc; có thể nói đến vật vắng mặt); D là bẫy từ khóa 'tiếng nói'.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

In discussing possible effects on "domains of thought," the author's stance is best described as
options: A. measured, underlining how far the evidence can and cannot be pushed.
B. dismissive, treating the whole idea as groundless speculation.
C. alarmed, insisting that late learners are bound to fail.
D. indifferent, viewing the question as beside the point.
questions.explanation: Tác giả rào đón kỹ ('các nhà nghiên cứu rất thận trọng', 'theo lập luận của một số người') và bác bỏ ý người học muộn 'vô vọng'. C nói ngược chính điều đó; B và D không khớp với việc tác giả vẫn coi vấn đề là quan trọng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

The passage states all of the following about established sign languages such as ASL EXCEPT that they
options: A. have grammatical systems of their own.
B. are handed down within a community of users.
C. vary from one region or nation to another.
D. are simply the local spoken language rendered by hand.
questions.explanation: Bài bác bỏ đúng phương án D như một 'ngộ nhận dai dẳng': ngôn ngữ ký hiệu không phải phiên bản bằng tay của tiếng nói. A, B, C đều là những điều bài khẳng định là đúng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

The discussion of the "sensitive period" most strongly implies that
options: A. a first language can be mastered fully at any age given enough effort.
B. a cochlear implant erases every disadvantage of late exposure.
C. when exposure first happens, not just how much of it, shapes the result.
D. signed languages are picked up faster than spoken ones.
questions.explanation: Ý 'một sự sẵn sàng mà về sau não không lấy lại được' cho thấy thời điểm sớm mới là yếu tố quyết định. A nói ngược; B bị bài phản bác vì tiếng nói nghe muộn cũng kém hoàn chỉnh; D không được bài đề cập.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

What does the passage imply about the past policy of suppressing signing in schools?
options: A. It frequently denied children the accessible language they most required.
B. It succeeded in improving spoken language for most pupils.
C. It rested on sound evidence that research later confirmed.
D. It had little real effect because children went on signing anyway.
questions.explanation: Bài nói chính sách ấy 'nhìn lại thường đã tước đi của trẻ đúng cái thứ… mà các em cần nhất'. B và C nói ngược tinh thần phê phán của tác giả; D suy diễn thêm điều bài không khẳng định.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 2

Which statement best captures the "modern lesson" the passage draws?
options: A. Deaf children ought to be taught speech before any form of signing.
B. Homesign is enough as long as the family keeps using it consistently.
C. A single sign language should be standardised for use worldwide.
D. What counts is early, well-timed access to a whole language, through whatever channel works.
questions.explanation: Đoạn cuối chốt: cái cần không phải một phương thức cụ thể mà là sự đắm mình kịp thời trong một ngôn ngữ hoàn chỉnh. A và B nói ngược bài; C mâu thuẫn với ý ngôn ngữ ký hiệu không mang tính phổ quát.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

What is the main point the writer makes about Facebook?
options: A. It is on the verge of a sudden and total collapse.
B. It stays commercially strong while quietly ageing and shedding its youngest users.
C. It has already been overtaken by Snapchat in total membership.
D. It has stopped growing and now shrinks a little every year.
questions.explanation: Bài viết nhấn mạnh Facebook không sụp đổ ầm ĩ mà 'đang già đi': doanh thu và quy mô vẫn lớn nhưng lượng người dùng trẻ đang rời xa. Các phương án còn lại phóng đại hoặc trái với việc 'tổng số thành viên vẫn tăng đều'.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

According to the passage, which users engage with Facebook most actively?
options: A. University students who were the first to join the site.
B. Teenagers who share only with a small circle of friends.
C. People born after the middle of the 1990s.
D. Members of older generations, such as Gen X and the boomers.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 2 cho biết nhóm Thế hệ X và thế hệ bùng nổ dân số đăng nhập thường xuyên hơn và nán lại lâu hơn gần như mọi người sinh sau giữa thập niên 1990. Sinh viên là thời quá khứ; nhóm sinh sau 1990 lại là nhóm đang rời đi.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

In paragraph 2, the word "off-putting" is closest in meaning to:
options: A. unappealing and discouraging
B. difficult to understand at first
C. costly to keep using
D. reassuring and familiar
questions.explanation: Câu văn đối lập: những tính năng khiến người lớn tuổi 'an tâm' lại là thứ khiến người trẻ thấy 'off-putting', nên từ này mang nghĩa gây khó chịu, đẩy người ta ra xa. Phương án D là nghĩa trái ngược.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

In the final paragraph, "the second condition" refers to Facebook being:
options: A. hugely profitable in financial terms
B. loyally followed by advertisers
C. quietly out of fashion
D. the place where things happen
questions.explanation: Câu nói một công ty có thể vừa 'rất sinh lời' vừa 'lặng lẽ lỗi thời'; 'điều kiện thứ nhất' là sinh lời, nên 'điều kiện thứ hai' chính là việc lỗi thời/mất tính thời thượng.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

The passage identifies which of the following as a reason young people avoid Facebook?
options: A. The app has removed the ability to message friends.
B. The presence of relatives makes posting feel supervised.
C. It shows too few advertisements to stay interesting.
D. It is now available only to older members.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 3 nêu 'sự hiện diện đầy dò xét' của cô chú, thầy cô khiến mọi bài đăng như bị theo dõi. Phương án C ngược với thực tế (quá nhiều quảng cáo), A và D không được nói tới.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

The writer's attitude toward Facebook's future can best be described as:
options: A. cautiously uncertain rather than triumphant or dismissive
B. openly hostile and glad to see it fail
C. certain that it will vanish very soon
D. indifferent to whether it survives or not
questions.explanation: Tác giả kết luận bằng chữ 'thực sự chưa chắc chắn' và cân nhắc cả hai khả năng, cho thấy giọng điệu thận trọng. Bài không hả hê (B), không quả quyết nó sẽ biến mất (C), cũng không dửng dưng (D).

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

The passage mentions all of the following as reasons Snapchat appeals to young users EXCEPT:
options: A. messages disappear, easing the pressure to look polished
B. it is aimed at a few close friends rather than a large audience
C. communication feels playful and visual
D. it offers richer news feeds and marketplace listings
questions.explanation: Tin tức và mục rao bán là đặc điểm của Facebook (đoạn 2), không phải lý do hấp dẫn của Snapchat. Ba phương án còn lại đều được nêu ở đoạn 4.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

When the writer calls Facebook "the king", the point being made is that Facebook:
options: A. is run by one all-powerful owner
B. treats its members like loyal subjects
C. still leads by far in earnings and sheer size
D. is admired by the young above all its rivals
questions.explanation: Cụm 'ông vua' gắn liền với câu về doanh thu và quy mô khổng lồ, ám chỉ vị thế thống trị về thương mại. Phương án D trái với luận điểm rằng người trẻ đang rời đi.

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

The comparison of Facebook to "an attic stuffed with notifications" implies that, to young users, the platform seems:
options: A. cluttered with accumulated, unwanted material
B. valuable and worth preserving carefully
C. dangerous and unsafe to use
D. empty and only rarely updated
questions.explanation: Hình ảnh 'gác xép chất đầy thông báo chẳng ai yêu cầu' gợi cảm giác chật chội, bừa bộn, cũ kỹ với người trẻ. Phương án D ngược lại (đầy chứ không trống).

questions.content:
reading — Passage 3

Which statement best captures the passage's concluding judgement?
options: A. Commercial success guarantees Facebook lasting dominance.
B. Facebook has already lost both its profits and its audience.
C. Cultural decline can never affect a company's earnings.
D. Being profitable yet unfashionable may, in time, endanger the profits too.
questions.explanation: Đoạn cuối cảnh báo rằng 'điều kiện thứ hai' (lỗi thời) sớm muộn có xu hướng đe dọa 'điều kiện thứ nhất' (lợi nhuận). A và C mâu thuẫn với ý này, còn B phóng đại vì bài khẳng định Facebook vẫn còn sinh lời lớn.
